### Historical population size and growth rate

Breeding population sizes of recent years (2006 - 2026) are estimated from the model. @tbl-hist gives these estimates and the association 95% posterior credible interval for the YKD and ACP. We present only the current conditions model for the past estimates, because future ice conditions do not affect them. The lead scenarios differ in assumed exposure during 2008–2026, however, and the fitted survival estimates for that period differ slightly among them (see Conclusion). The population estimates for 2006–2026 under the other lead scenarios differ little from those presented and are available in the data supplement. 

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: tbl-hist
#| tbl-cap: "Breeding population size (pairs) as estimated from the integrated population model for the years 2016 to 2026." 
index <- 19:39
df <- data.frame(Year = 2006:2026, 
                 mYKD = post_current$mean$Nb[index]/2, 
                 medYKD = post_current$q50$Nb[index]/2,
                 ciYKD = paste0(round(post_current$q2.5$Nb[index]/2, 0), " - ", round(post_current$q97.5$Nb[index]/2, 0)),
                 mACP = ACP.current$mean$Nb[index]/2, 
                 medACP = ACP.current$q50$Nb[index]/2,
                 ciACP = paste0(round(ACP.current$q2.5$Nb[index]/2, 0), " - ", round(ACP.current$q97.5$Nb[index]/2, 0)))
kable(df, align = c("l", rep("c", 8)), col.names = c("Year", "Mean", "Median", "95% CI", 
                                                            "Mean", "Median", "95% CI"), 
      booktabs = TRUE, digits = 0, row.names = FALSE) |> 
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position") %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "YKD Breeding Population (pairs)" = 3, "ACP Breeding Population (pairs)" = 3)) 

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trend
#| tbl-cap: "Period-specific annual average growth rate for the YKD and ACP based on breeding population estimates from the intergrated population model. Lower and Upper are the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles for the posteror growth rate, respectively."

YKD.lambda <- (post_current$sims.list$Nb[,39]/post_current$sims.list$Nb[,1])^(1/39)

ACP.lambda <- (ACP.current$sims.list$Nb[,39]/ACP.current$sims.list$Nb[,20])^(1/19)

YKD.lambda19 <- (post_current$sims.list$Nb[,39]/post_current$sims.list$Nb[,20])^(1/19)

YKD.lambda10 <- (post_current$sims.list$Nb[,39]/post_current$sims.list$Nb[,29])^(1/10)

ACP.lambda10 <- (ACP.current$sims.list$Nb[,39]/ACP.current$sims.list$Nb[,29])^(1/10)

df_trend <- matrix(0, 38, 5)
lag <- 1:38
for( i in lag){
  tmp <- (post_current$sims.list$Nb[,39]/post_current$sims.list$Nb[,39 - i])^(1/i)
  df_trend[i,1] <- i
  df_trend[i, 2] <- mean(tmp)
  df_trend[i, 3] <- quantile(tmp, probs = 0.5)
  df_trend[i, 4] <- quantile(tmp, probs = 0.025)
  df_trend[i, 5] <- quantile(tmp, probs = 0.975)
}
df_trend <- as.data.frame(df_trend)
period <- paste0(2026, " - ", (2025:1988))
df_trend <- mutate(df_trend, Period = period, .after = 1)
names(df_trend) <- c("Lag", "Period", "Mean", "Median", "Lower", "Upper")
df_trend_YKD <- df_trend
# kable(df_trend_YKD, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c","c", "c"), 
#       digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE)
#Now for ACP
df_trend <- matrix(0, 19, 5)
lag <- 1:19
for( i in lag){
  tmp <- (ACP.current$sims.list$Nb[,39]/ACP.current$sims.list$Nb[,39 - i])^(1/i)
  df_trend[i,1] <- i
  df_trend[i, 2] <- mean(tmp)
  df_trend[i, 3] <- quantile(tmp, probs = 0.5)
  df_trend[i, 4] <- quantile(tmp, probs = 0.025)
  df_trend[i, 5] <- quantile(tmp, probs = 0.975)
}
df_trend <- as.data.frame(df_trend)
period <- paste0(2026, " - ", (2025:2007))
df_trend <- mutate(df_trend, Period = period, .after = 1)
names(df_trend) <- c("Lag", "Period", "Mean", "Median", "Lower", "Upper")
df_trend_ACP <- df_trend
# kable(df_trend_ACP, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c","c", "c"), 
#       digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE)
df_trend_ACP <- df_trend_ACP[1:nrow(df_trend_YKD), , drop = FALSE]
df_trend <- cbind(df_trend_YKD, df_trend_ACP[,-c(1:2)])
kable(df_trend, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", rep("c", 9))) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "YKD" = 4, "ACP" = 4))
```

The estimated average growth rate for each population is a second derived quantity of interest. This is estimated from the posterior breeding population size,

$$\lambda_{t_2-t_1} = (n_{b,t_2}/n_{b,t_1})^{1/(t_2-t_1)} $$

For the YKD population, average growth rate from 1988 to 2026 was `r round(quantile(YKD.lambda, 0.5), 3)`, 95% CI: `r round(quantile(YKD.lambda, 0.025), 3)` - `r round(quantile(YKD.lambda, 0.975), 3)`, reflecting a population that is now at or below the population in 1988 before the species was listed (@fig-counts, @tbl-trend). Across the years 2007 to 2026 (to be consistent with the ACP time period), the average growth rate for the YKD population was `r round(quantile(YKD.lambda19, 0.5), 3)`, 95% CI: `r round(quantile(YKD.lambda19, 0.025), 3)` - `r round(quantile(YKD.lambda19, 0.975), 3)`, reflecting a decline from 2007 (@fig-counts2, @tbl-trend). Across the years 2007 to 2026, the average growth rate for the ACP population was `r round(quantile(ACP.lambda, 0.5), 3)`, 95% CI: `r round(quantile(ACP.lambda, 0.025), 3)` - `r round(quantile(ACP.lambda, 0.975), 3)`, also reflecting a decline from 2007 (@fig-counts2). Note that these growth rates average across the time period; thus, averaging over any dynamics within the period. This is especially important for the YKD population where there was a long increasing trend followed by a quick decrease to near the initial condition in 1988 (@fig-counts). For example, if the time period is shortened to 10 years, the growth rate become even more negative for the YKD (`r paste0(round(quantile(YKD.lambda10, 0.5), 3), ", 95% CI: ", round(quantile(YKD.lambda10, 0.025), 3), " - ", round(quantile(YKD.lambda10, 0.975), 3))`, @tbl-trend) but are less affected for the ACP (`r round(quantile(ACP.lambda10, 0.5), 3)`, 95% CI: `r round(quantile(ACP.lambda10, 0.025), 3)` - `r round(quantile(ACP.lambda10, 0.975), 3)`). 

### Future population size

Estimated future population sizes for the YKD and ACP at 2066 and 2100 under all climate and lead scenarios for the vague (baseline) prior are shown in @tbl-popykd and @tbl-popacp, respectively. Note that there is extreme variation for each scenario, especially for the YKD and at 2100, and extreme skew (note the difference between the mean and median at any time point). This is due largely to the increased extinction probability (for all scenarios) and due to the uncertain effect of ice on survival, where under some decreased ice scenarios, carrying capacity (and thus, the upper bound on population size) is increased with reduced ice. These effects increase the skew of the population size posterior at any time point due to some simulations resulting in extinction while others lead to large population size. This causes a large difference between the posterior mean and median. For these reasons, the median and 95 percent CI are probability better representations of the posterior. 

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: tbl-popykd
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated future breeding population size at 2066 and 2100 for the YKD population under alternative scenarios of ice projections and lead exposure under the vague prior on the effect of ice on survival. Given are the posterior mean, posterior median, posterior probability the population is > 5000 (Pr(> 5K)), posterior probability the population is > 10,000 (Pr(> 10K)), and 95% CI. "

summarize_years_wide <- function(posteriors, years) {
  # posteriors : named list of posterior matrices (rows = MCMC samples, cols = years)
  # years      : vector of column indices to summarize, e.g. c(t1, t2)
  # Returns a data frame: one row per scenario, columns = <stat>_yr<year>

  stat_fun <- function(x) {
    c(mean   = mean(x),
      median = median(x),
      p5000 = mean(x > 5000),
      p10000 = mean(x > 10000),
      q2.5   = quantile(x, 0.025, names = FALSE),
      q97.5  = quantile(x, 0.975, names = FALSE))
  }

  mat <- t(sapply(posteriors, function(m) {
    # apply stats to each requested year, then flatten to a named vector
    s <- apply(m[, years, drop = FALSE], 2, stat_fun)  # rows = stat, cols = year
    stats <- rownames(s)
    out <- as.vector(s)                                 # flattens column-major
    names(out) <- paste0(rep(stats, times = length(years)),
                         "_yr", rep(years, each = length(stats)))
    out
  }))

  df <- data.frame(scenario = rownames(mat), mat, row.names = NULL,
                   check.names = FALSE)
  df
}

# Example
#tbl <- summarize_years_wide(posteriors, c(1, 10))
NBresults <- summarize_years_wide(posteriors, c(79, 113))
NBresults <- mutate(NBresults, across(c(2:3, 6:9, 12:13), round, digits = 0)) |>
  mutate(across(c(4:5, 10:11), round, digits = 2))
df <- data.frame(Scenario = c("Current Conditions", 
                 "RCP 4.5 - Lead 2008", 
                 "RCP 4.5 - Lead 2026",
                 "RCP 4.5 - Lead Constant",
                 "RCP 8.5 - Lead 2008", 
                 "RCP 8.5 - Lead 2026",
                 "RCP 8.5 - Lead Constant", 
                 "Current Conditions", 
                 "RCP 4.5", 
                 "RCP 8.5"),
                 Mean66 = NBresults[,2], Median66 = NBresults[,3],
                 "Pr(> 5K)" = NBresults[,4], "Pr(> 10K)" = NBresults[,5],
                 "95%CI66" = paste0(NBresults[,6], " - ", NBresults[,7]),
                 Mean74 = NBresults[,8], Median74 = NBresults[,9],
                 "Pr(> 5K)" = NBresults[,10], "Pr(> 10K)" = NBresults[,11],
                 "95%CI74" = paste0(NBresults[,12], " - ", NBresults[,13]))
library(kableExtra)
kable(df[1:7,], align = c("l", rep("c", 10)), col.names = c("Scenario", "Mean", "Median", "Pr(> 5K)", "Pr(> 10K)", "95% CI", 
                                                            "Mean", "Median", "Pr(> 5K)", "Pr(> 10K)", "95% CI"), 
      row.names = FALSE, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "scale_down") |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "2066 Breeding Population" = 5, "2100 Breeding Population" = 5))
```

Population projections for the YKD are summarized in @fig-projYKD. These show the effect of lead scenario (along columns), the effect climate scenario (along rows), and for two priors on the effect of ice deviations on survival. The top four plots of @fig-projYKD show projections for a less informed survival prior where survival can increase with deviations from mean historical ice, and the bottom four plots show projections for a more informed prior that does not allow for increases in survival with deviations in ice. There is a large effect of the specified prior on population projections, and therefore extinction probability and probability of any future population size. Because the informed prior imposes a large constraint on the posterior beyond any likelihood from the data, this shows how the current data do not inform of relationship between ice and survival. Results from this specification show the effect of restricting the ice effect to concave-down. To the degree that this prior is believed to be biologically more realistic, the result from this model should receive greater weight. 

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-projYKD
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Estimated mean population projections for the Y-K Delta breeding population (dark grey line) under alternative lead  and winter sea ice condition (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) scenarios and two different priors on survival. Columns indicate lead scenario as constant (A, C, E, and G) or declining after 2026 (B, D, F, and H). Rows indicate sea ice conditions as RCP 4.5 (A, B, E, and F) or RCP 8.5 (C, D, G, and H). Plots A through D show the less-informed prior on suvival where surival can increase with deviations from mean ice, and plots E through H show results for a more informed prior where suvival can only decreased with deviations from mean ice. 95% credibility intervals given by the light grey areas. Observed counts (± 1 SE) are shown in each panel as points and error bars. Red lines indicate population levels associated with resilience criteria (N = 5,000 and 10,000). Note that some trajectories go to population sizes > 40,000, but the plot is truncated at that value."

plot_pop <- function(post, counts){
  df <- data.frame(Year = 1988:2100,
                   Mean = apply(post, 2, mean), 
                   upper = apply(post, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.975)),
                   lower = apply(post, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025)))
  
  p <- ggplot(data = df, aes(x = Year, y = Mean)) + 
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin= lower, ymax = upper), fill = "lightgray") + 
    geom_line(col = "darkgray", size = 1) + 
    geom_pointrange(data = counts, 
                    aes(x = Year, y = Nibb, ymin = Nibb - seNibb, ymax = Nibb + seNibb), linewidth = 0.25, size = 0.2) + 
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(5000, 10000), col = "red") + 
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 40000)) +
    labs(y = "Population") + 
    theme_classic() 
  return(p)
}

counts <- filter(counts.YKD, filtered == 0 & ! is.na(Nibb))
p1 <- plot_pop(post = posteriors$YKD.constant.4.5, counts = counts)
p2 <- plot_pop(post = posteriors$YKD.L2026.4.5, counts = counts)
p3 <- plot_pop(post = posteriors$YKD.constant.8.5, counts = counts)
p4 <- plot_pop(post = posteriors$YKD.L2026.8.5, counts = counts)
p5 <- plot_pop(post = posteriors2$YKD.constant.4.5, counts = counts)
p6 <- plot_pop(post = posteriors2$YKD.L2026.4.5, counts = counts)
p7 <- plot_pop(post = posteriors2$YKD.constant.8.5, counts = counts)
p8 <- plot_pop(post = posteriors2$YKD.L2026.8.5, counts = counts)
(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4) / (p5 + p6) / (p7 + p8) + 
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'A')

ggsave("figures/projYKD.svg")
ggsave("figures/projYKD.png")
ggsave("figures/projYKD.pdf")
```

### 2023 Russian population estimate

```{r}
tot <- readRDS(file = "MS_Scenarios/jm2.RDS")$sims.list$N_population |>
  sample(10000)
ykd_tot <- readRDS(file = "MS_Scenarios/YKD.current.rds")$sims.list$Ntot[sample(10000)]
acp_tot <- readRDS(file = "MS_Scenarios/ACP.current.rds")$sims.list$Ntot[sample(10000)]
russ <- tot - ykd_tot - acp_tot

df <- data.frame(mtot = mean(tot), medtot = quantile(tot, probs = c(0.5)),
                   totup = quantile(tot, probs = c(0.975)), 
                   totlow = quantile(tot, probs = c(0.025)), 
                 mykd = mean(ykd_tot), ykdup = quantile(ykd_tot, probs = c(0.975)), 
                   ykdlow = quantile(ykd_tot, probs = c(0.025)), 
                 macp = mean(acp_tot), acpup = quantile(acp_tot, probs = c(0.975)), 
                   acplow = quantile(acp_tot, probs = c(0.025)), 
                 mruss = mean(russ), medruss = quantile(russ, probs = c(0.5)),
                   russup = quantile(russ, probs = c(0.975)), 
                   russlow = quantile(russ, probs = c(0.025)))
options(scipen = 999)
```

Given the total population size (as individuals including juveniles, non-breeders, and breeding adults) of the wintering world population in March of 2023 (mean: `r round(df$mtot, 0)`, median: `r round(df$medtot, 0)`, 95% CI: `r round(df$totlow, 0)` - `r round(df$totup, 0)`), and the total population in June of the YKD (mean: `r round(df$mykd, 0)`, 95% CI: `r round(df$ykdlow, 0)` - `r round(df$ykdup, 0)`) and ACP (mean: `r round(df$macp, 0)`, 95% CI: `r round(df$acplow, 0)` - `r round(df$acpup, 0)`), the Russian population size is estimated as a posterior mean of `r round(df$mruss, 0)` (median: `r round(df$medruss, 0)`, 95% CI: `r round(df$russlow, 0)` - `r round(df$russup, 0)`). Note the skew in the estimates of the total world population and the Russian population. Because of this skew, the median and 95 percent CI are a better representation of the posterior than the mean alone. This calculation is slightly biased by the mortality between March and June, but given the relatively high survival of these eiders in a typical year, this is a very small bias, especially relative to the uncertainty in the total world population estimate. 

## Conclusion

The main conclusions from this version of the PVA are: (1) extinction probabilities for both populations are much larger and non-trivial compared to 2021 due to a large decline in population size; (2) The effect of winter ice cover on survival is less certain than previously thought (circa 2021), and this uncertainty has major practical consequences for the population projections and extinction probability estimates. For YKD adult survival, the posterior for the quadratic ice effect is now centered near zero (mean −0.01, 95% CI −0.16 to 0.15), with a posterior probability of 0.53 that the effect is negative. A large proportion of the posterior therefore allows survival to increase with deviations from historical mean ice. Together with the weaker density dependence, this allows population size to reach large values in some future simulations, which lowers extinction risk in those simulations.

Because the data do not determine the shape of the survival–ice relationship, the results depend on the prior. We present two specifications that differ in their assumptions about curvature:  

 - The baseline prior is centered on zero and agnostic about curvature. It places half its mass on concave-up relationships, which some consider biologically unlikely, and the data shift it very little.
 - The informed prior restricts curvature to concave-down, so survival cannot increase with deviations from mean ice. This is consistent with expert consensus on breeding propensity. Experts were not asked directly about survival. 
 
The informed prior gave higher QE and lower projected abundance than the baseline prior in every scenario. The relative increase in QE ranged from about 13% to 70% and varied among scenarios. Because the data contribute little to curvature, this difference reflects the priors, not the data. The two specifications should be read as contrasting curvature assumptions at the prior scale used here. They are not bounds on QE. The informed prior is the more pessimistic of the two, but it is concentrated near zero, i.e., no curvature. Its posterior mean quadratic effect is −0.068 for both populations. A stronger negative ice effect would give higher QE than either specification. The ordering of the two sets of results depends on the prior scale and on the weak information in the data about curvature. Other omitted processes, such as demographic stochasticity and mass-mortality events, mean neither set of results is an upper limit on risk. Which prior to use is a matter of expert biological judgment. To the extent that a concave-down effect is considered appropriate for survival, as it was for breeding propensity, the informed-prior results should be given greater weight.

The models presented here represent much weaker density-dependence than used in 2021. This is due to a change in prior specification that is considered more biologically plausible and better matches the expert elicitation results. The consequence is that the models presented here will produce larger population sizes and *lower* extinction probabilities than the models used in 2021. That is, if the 2021 models were fit to the current (circa 2026) data, extinction probabilities would likely be *higher* than presented here, all else equal. Given that 40-year quasi-extinction probabilities were < 1 percent for all populations and scenarios in 2021, refitting the current model to those data would likely cause even *lower* extinction probabilities. Thus, the large increase in QE probabilities presented here is not simply due to differences in model structure or priors, it is therefore due in substantial part to the reduced population sizes, although the larger variance in annual survival may also contribute. 

The lead scenarios represent assumptions about lead exposure, not estimates from lead data. No lead exposure data enter the likelihood. The initial exposure rate, its decay rate and the relative survival of exposed birds are set by priors based on Flint et al. (2016), and the Kigigak survival data cannot separate them from the survival intercept, ice effects, density dependence and annual random effects. The relative survival prior also assumes that all survival differences between Kigigak and Kashunuk were caused by lead, which is a maximum attribution. Within the model, the lead effect on adult survival is modest, with breeder survival reduced by at most about 6% in relative terms and by less once exposure declines. Survival differences of a few percentage points do accumulate over decades, which is why QE is highest when lead is held constant.

The lead scenarios also differ in assumed exposure during 2008–2026, a period covered by the survival data. Each scenario is therefore a separate model fit with a different hypothesis about the recent past, and not only a different projection. We hypothesize that this explains the unexpected result that QE and median abundance were not worse under Lead 2026 than under Lead 2008 (@fig-medYKD, @tbl-qeykd, @tbl-popykd). Where high exposure is assumed through the data period, the same observed survival is attributed partly to lead, so the fitted lead-free survival is higher. Consistent with this, the survival intercepts were higher under the Lead 2026 and Constant scenarios, by about 0.01 - 0.013 at the posterior mean. When lead declines in the projection period, survival under Lead 2026 therefore recovers from a higher baseline, and the change in adult survival from 2026 to 2030 was largest under this scenario. These differences carry forward and interact with density dependence and climate to produce different trajectories. We did not monitor the lead parameters, so we could not confirm that their posteriors differ among scenarios, and the explanation remains a hypothesis. A similar pattern occurred in the 2021 analysis. It may have been less apparent then because the larger population size, stronger density dependence, and strong ice effects could have produced a larger near-term lead effect in the projections, but that has not been verified. The result is not necessarily a model error. It reflects how the scenarios are defined and how they interact with the model fit. Differences among lead scenarios should be read as conditional illustrations of the possible benefit of reducing lead, not as predictions or as evidence of how much lead has affected the populations. Contemporary blood lead measurements from the YKD would do the most to constrain these results, and monitoring the lead parameters in future runs would test the hypothesis fully.

Both Alaska populations have been in decline. For the ACP, this decline has averaged over 10-20 years at around 4% per year with recent year being constant (@tbl-trend, @fig-counts2). For the YKD, this decline has been localized to two recent periods (around 2020 and between June 2024 and June 2025) and both have been roughly half or more of the observed population with relative stasis otherwise (@fig-counts). Over the last 10 years, the *average* decline in the YDK population has been 13% per year (@tbl-trend), which is itself an extreme decline. If only one or two more periods of such high-magnitude decline are realized, the number of eiders on the YKD will only a few 100s of pairs, not 1000s. It is further alarming that these high-magnitude declines have occurred in the most recent years, and not throughout the history of monitoring this species. If such an abrupt regime shift has occurred in the frequency of mortality events, then the extinction probabilities presented here are biased low, perhaps very low. The models include annual random effects on survival, with a variance that is likely constrained by its prior, and these can produce occasional low-survival years. They do not include a change in the frequency or persistence of such events. Such regime shifts should be considered when interpreting model results presented here and determining species status for ESA listing. 

The projections include environmental variation through annual random effects on survival and fecundity, but they omit demographic stochasticity, the variation arising from chance outcomes of individual survival and reproduction. This was less important in the 2021 analysis, when the populations were larger and the main question was recovery toward delisting. It is more relevant now that the YKD breeding population is estimated at 1,410 pairs in 2026 and the quasi-extinction threshold is 250 breeding individuals (about 125 pairs). Demographic variance in population growth scales as 1/N, so it is largest near the threshold. A rough calculation suggests that, at the threshold, it is as large as the year-to-year environmental variation seen before 2019 (assuming a per-capita demographic variance of 0.3–1.0), and a simple simulation indicated that it would increase quasi-extinction probabilities by only a few thousandths to about 0.01 in absolute terms. Demographic stochasticity alone is therefore unlikely to account for a large bias, although this was not evaluated within the integrated model.

A larger concern is environmental variation. The posterior for the standard deviation of the annual random effect on adult survival is concentrated at the upper bound of its Uniform(0, 1) prior, which indicates that the data support at least as much unexplained year-to-year variation as the prior allowed. This is consistent with the 2020–21 and 2024–25 YKD declines. Because the random effects are carried into the projections, they allow occasional years of very low survival. For illustration, with mean survival near 0.84 and a standard deviation of 1.0 on the logit scale, about 1% of years would have survival below 0.35, ignoring other covariates. The projections therefore include some crash-like variation, but as independent normal draws, not as a separate process, and the variance is probably capped by the prior. The projections cannot represent changes in the frequency or clustering of such events. Both features suggest that the quasi-extinction probabilities are biased low, by an amount that was not quantified. Future versions should relax the bound on this standard deviation, add demographic stochasticity, and evaluate scenarios with a specified frequency of large mortality events.

The Russian population is relatively large. However, 2023 represents the first scientifically rigorous population estimate, so a trend cannot be estimated directly. The model assumes correlated demography between the two Alaska populations, implemented through a shared mark-recapture likelihood. Because the Russian population overwinters in the same environment, its demography may also be correlated with the Alaska populations. Under such a correlation, the Russian population may have been much larger before 2023 (if it shared the 2020–21 YKD crash), and it may now be substantially smaller than estimated in 2023 (if it shared the 2024–25 YKD crash). The 2023 estimate falls between these two events. The evidence for a shared response is mixed. The ACP declined during 2019–2022, when the YKD declined, but it has been stable since 2022 and showed no counterpart to the 2024–25 YKD crash, suggesting that any correlation is partial. These possibilities cannot be distinguished because earlier wintering estimates were only minimum counts with many sources of error. Because the YKD and, until recently, the ACP have declined, the possibility that the Russian population is also declining should be given reasonable consideration in determining ESA listing status, although the available data cannot confirm it.
